literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's the first of November, and this weekend's reading news is dominated by the Booker Prize, with some lovely detours into writers' lives, poetry, music and a little gothic mystery.

Let me begin with the Booker, since so much has been written about it. The Conversation has brought together six experts to review the twenty twenty-six nominees, and their argument is that the list is diverse enough to inspire all sorts of readers. It's a useful place to start if you want real critical substance rather than a simple roll call. The Independent, meanwhile, has a piece on what it was like for this year's judges to read one hundred and sixty-three books in seven months. Only the headline reached me, so I can't tell you what they say about the experience, but the number alone is a small marvel. And News24 has a guide to the titles in the running, again in summary form, which may serve as a handy checklist.

Two individual novels are getting attention. Gayety reviews Marlon James's shortlisted novel The Disappearers, which follows gay men in Kingston after an attack in nineteen eighty-eight. It sounds like a historical novel with a strong premise and a clear narrative focus, the sort of book that might teach a period through people rather than dates. The Michigan Daily, a student paper, has a review of May We Feed The King by Rebecca Perry, another Booker nominee. The excerpt I have is too short to say anything about its style, but it's one to look up if the title has caught your ear. And a related note: the South African novelist Damon Galgut, himself a Booker winner, has been awarded the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award. I only have the headline, but it's pleasant news for a writer already well honoured.

Now to writers and their lineages, which I thought you might enjoy. Prospect Magazine considers the many revolutions of John Berger, whose work moved between art criticism, fiction and politics. The text I have is brief, but for anyone who loves the meeting of painting and prose, Berger is surely the patron saint, and the piece looks promising. In The Hindu, the novelist Elif Shafak talks about the kindred spirit she found in Gustave Flaubert. It's an interview about the affinity between a living writer and an earlier master of the novel, and I like the idea of choosing one's literary ancestors that way.

The Guardian, for its part, has an interview with Helen Garner, the Australian writer of unsparing fiction and true crime. She talks about surviving three marriages, being called a rotten feminist, and finding global recognition five decades into her career. The headline quotes her saying that being hated is very bracing, which gives you a sense of her frank, self-possessed voice. It looks like a fine portrait of a narrator's temperament as much as a writer's. The Guardian's monthly round-up, in which Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and readers share what they enjoyed in October, also includes a recommendation of James Bailey's biography of Muriel Spark, praised for its detail and readability. Spark is always a good companion, so that may be one for the winter evenings.

Turning to language and sound. The New York Times reviews two new poetry collections that lean into the ecstatic, aiming for almost mystical effects. If you are in the mood for poetry that is beautiful simply as language, that may be the piece to read. The same paper also reviews Sound Tracks by Graeme Lawson, which tells a story of human music-making through ancient instruments. It blends music, archaeology and history, and there's something wonderful in the thought of the oldest music being pieced together from objects that survive. It might even sit nicely beside one of your classical music documentaries.

For something darker, the New York Times also reviews Our Cut of Salt by Deena Helm, in which a young woman returns to her ancestral home and uncovers chilling secrets. It has the gothic, mysterious shape that suits a thriller lover, with a returning narrator at its heart. In a gentler, more period key, Livemint reviews a novel by Nisar Aziz Butt about a life-loving young woman in the nineteen fifties. I only have the headline, but a character-led story with a historical setting could be just the sort of book you can step into without needing to know the culture first.

Finally, a good tip for finding voices beyond English. The Guardian has a roundup of recent translated fiction. It features Barbi Marković's eccentric, fantastical micro-fictions in Minihorror, along with new books by Pol Guasch, Helle Helle and Hamid Ismailov. Marković's sound especially playful, and the roundup is a convenient way to sample four quite different writers at once.

So there's plenty to browse, whether you're after a prize contender, a biography or a ghost in the attic, and I hope a quiet Sunday up in Les Adrets gives you time to start one of them.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's the first of November, and the last couple of days have brought a good crop of writing about writers: how they live, who they borrow from, and what a prize does to the books it gathers up.

Let me begin with the Booker Prize, which dominates the week. The Conversation has pulled together six experts to review the 2026 nominees, and the argument running through the piece is that this is a diverse list, one that should find readers of quite different tastes. I like the format. Six separate readers, each taking a book on its own terms, tend to give you more than one critic summing up a whole list. If you want a way into the year's prize without committing to every title, it looks like a sound place to start.

Alongside it, The Independent has a piece asking what it was like for this year's judges to read one hundred and sixty-three books in seven months. I should be honest that only the headline reached me, so I can't tell you what the judges said about it. But the number alone is striking. One hundred and sixty-three books in seven months is a very particular kind of reading life, and I'd be curious whether it changes how you read, as well as how much. And News24 offers a guide to the titles still in the running, described as the unmissable ones. Again, only a summary headline came through, but it points to a handy overview if you'd like the whole field laid out.

Two individual books from the list are getting attention. Gayety reviews Marlon James's The Disappearers, which is Booker-shortlisted. It follows gay men in Kingston after an attack in nineteen eighty-eight. That is a historical novel with a very clear focus: a specific place, a specific year, and a community living in the aftermath of violence. For someone who loves novels that teach history better than history essays do, that setup is promising. A single event, seen through the people who had to live beyond it, is often how fiction gets under the skin of a period. I can only tell you what the review establishes about the premise, but the premise is strong.

The other is Rebecca Perry's May We Feed The King, a Booker Prize nominee, covered by The Michigan Daily. It's a student-paper review, and the excerpt is too short for me to say anything about the prose or the voice. What I can say is that it's a reminder of how widely this list is being read and discussed, down to university papers. I'd treat it as a title to note down rather than one I can describe.

There's also a note of prize news from further afield. The South African novelist Damon Galgut, himself a Booker winner, has won the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award. The Korea Herald item is only a headline, so there's no detail on the citation or the book. Still, it's a nice piece of recognition travelling across continents, and good news is always welcome.

Now to the part of the week I suspect you'll enjoy most: writers talking about themselves and about each other.

In The Guardian, there's an interview with Helen Garner, the Australian writer of unsparing fiction and true crime. The headline is a gift in itself: being hated, she says, is very bracing. The conversation covers her three marriages, the time she was called a rotten feminist, and the fact that global recognition has come to her five decades into her career. I find that last point quite moving. So many writers are celebrated early and then fade; here is one whose widest audience has arrived after fifty years of work. The interview is described as frank and self-possessed, and that sounds like exactly the voice you'd want from a writer whose books refuse to flatter anyone. If you're ever looking for a real-life example of a memorable narrator's temperament, someone who has been disliked and carried on regardless, this seems to offer it.

The Hindu, meanwhile, has an interview with Elif Shafak about the kindred spirit she found in Gustave Flaubert. I only have the framing, not the detail of what she says, but the idea is a lovely one: a living novelist feeling an affinity with an earlier one, as if literary lineage were a kind of friendship across time. It's the sort of thing that could make a good prompt for older pupils. Which writers do we feel close to, and why? Do we choose them, or do they find us?

And Prospect Magazine considers the many revolutions of John Berger, the writer whose work moved between art criticism, fiction and politics. The text I have is brief, so I can't take you through the argument. But the title alone suggests the very thing you care about: a writer who refused to keep painting, storytelling and political thought in separate rooms. Berger is exactly the kind of figure through whom you can think about how images and words speak to each other, so it's one to save for a quieter moment.

Staying with lives of writers, The Guardian's monthly round-up, What we're reading, has Ian Rankin, Louise Kennedy and Guardian readers sharing what they enjoyed in October. One pick stands out: James Bailey's biography of Muriel Spark, praised for its detail and its readability. A biography that is both thorough and a pleasure to read is rarer than it ought to be, and it makes a good companion to the Garner interview. Between them, you have a living writer reflecting on her own life, and a biographer reconstructing another's. It's also a friendly sort of piece, because it's people simply recommending books they loved, which is perhaps the best reason to read anything.

Turning to music, The New York Times reviews Graeme Lawson's Sound Tracks, which tells a story of human music-making through ancient instruments. It blends music, archaeology and history, and it seems to ask what we can learn about people from the things they made in order to make sound. Given your love of classical music and of history told in human terms, I think this is a natural fit. There is something wonderful about the idea of instruments as a kind of testimony, objects that carry the trace of people who wanted to sing, or play, or be heard.

The same section of The New York Times also has a review of two new poetry collections that lean into the ecstatic, aiming for almost mystical effects. The detail of which poets and which lines isn't in what I have, so I can't quote anything. But ecstatic poetry is an interesting thing to bring to a classroom, because it dares to be excessive in a way that most modern writing is nervous about. If any of the lines turn out to be as musical as the review suggests, they might be good to read aloud.

For something with a darker edge, there's Deena Helm's Our Cut of Salt, reviewed in The New York Times. A young woman returns to her ancestral home and uncovers chilling secrets. That is the classic gothic shape: the house, the inheritance, the narrator who comes back and begins to see what was always hidden. It's also the structure of a good thriller, and a returning narrator is a powerful device because she is both an insider and a stranger. If you want a book for a long autumn evening up in Les Adrets, with the mountains darkening outside, this sounds like it was written for that mood.

Finally, two pieces about voices from elsewhere. The Guardian has a roundup of the best recent translated fiction. It highlights Barbi Marković's Minihorror, described as eccentric, fantastical micro-fictions, plus new books by Pol Guasch, Helle Helle and Hamid Ismailov. I like the sound of micro-fictions that are both eccentric and slightly frightening; short forms can be brilliant for teaching, because a whole strange world can fit in a page. And the roundup is a good way to find a strong voice from outside English, which seems fitting for a week in which prizes and interviews have ranged from Kingston to Korea to Australia.

And from Livemint, a review of a novel by Nisar Aziz Butt, about a life-loving young woman in the nineteen-fifties. Only the headline reached me, so I can't speak to the style. But a character-led story with a period setting, and a heroine defined by her appetite for life, is a promising combination, and it's a reminder of how much fiction there is that can be stepped into without needing to know the culture first.

So, in short: a Booker season in full swing, some lovely conversations between writers and their forebears, and a few books that could fill a dark evening nicely.

That's the shelf for today, Yamuna, and I hope something on it follows you home.

art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle Sunday for art news, with a few good things close to home and some lovely stories where paintings meet words.

Let me begin in Grenoble, where the Musée de Grenoble has a run of talks and events. Tomorrow, Monday the second of November, at half past two, there is a free lecture for the Friends of the Museum on a work called "La Victorieuse", or "La Martiale", from Le Caire. It's a chance to look closely at a single piece from the collection, and if you're able to go, it might be worth seeing the work itself beforehand, so the talk has something to land on. Then on Wednesday the fourth, at half past six, another Friends of the Museum lecture takes up the Book of Revelation, read as visions, terror and consolation. For someone who teaches literature, that is a rich subject, since few texts have fed the imagination of painters so powerfully. Looking further ahead, from Monday the twenty-third to Sunday the twenty-ninth of November, there's a Clair-Obscur event with the collective Ici-Même, also at the museum. The listing gives little detail beyond the dates, but it's one to keep in your diary. The flash visits of the collection were yesterday afternoon, so that moment has passed.

A little closer to Les Adrets, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that the Y'a tout ça festival in Lans-en-Vercors is being extended into an exhibition. The report is brief, so I can't tell you more than that it exists, but it's a local show and easy to look into.

Now to one of the most charming stories of the weekend. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's "The Starry Night". It's a lovely link between astronomy and one of the best-loved canvases in the world, and an invitation to look again at those swirling skies, perhaps with a new sense of what he might actually have been seeing from his window. It could make a good starting point for a class, a painter's vision set beside a real night sky.

Staying with painting and writing, The Guardian's weekly round-up of art has a mention of the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge, which is showing an exhibition on late Victorian art and politics. William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites are at its heart, and the show runs until the third of May. It's a good reminder that for Morris, writing, design and painting were never really separate, and that the pre-Raphaelites drew so much from poetry and legend. The same round-up also takes in Orkney and a Halloween-flavoured piece from Derry, if you want to browse it.

Over in Paris, the Musée Jacquemart-André is devoted to the Venetian painter Tintoretto in a major exhibition. The report from mesinfos is short, so I can't give you dates or details of what's on show, but it's worth checking the museum's own pages if you're heading to the capital. And a digital-museum exhibition called "L'Impressionnisme: sur les traces de Claude Monet" follows the painter's path. The text I have is thin, but it may be of interest if you'd like a way into Monet from your own sofa.

For something with real depth, The Guardian has a long feature on Geoffrey Bardon and the painters of Papunya. It examines the myth surrounding the beginnings of Western Desert Aboriginal dot painting, a movement that has become world famous, and asks who is really credited with its origins. A new biography prompts this fresh look, and the piece sets out the history in a way that questions the neat story we've often been told. It's a substantial read, about how a story gets told around an art movement, which is something a literature teacher will appreciate.

On the literary side, BBC Radio 4's Front Row has an episode with Audrey Niffenegger, talking about "Life Out of Order", the sequel to her hugely successful novel "The Time Traveller's Wife". She returns to the time-travelling father and daughter, and it's always interesting to hear a writer go back to characters who have lived so long in readers' minds. The same programme also covers Kyle MacLachlan's memoir and has a segment on Dracula's long literary history, which should make for a rich listen, especially at this time of year.

And to finish, a few pieces in pictures, all light and from The Guardian. Mark McEvoy describes his best phone picture, taken in a shop in Margate in 2014, of a young woman in a fur coat, where a gust of wind blowing back her hair, he says, added something special. It's a small, human story about catching a moment. There's also a photo essay on Japan's "Jimi Halloween", a Tokyo event where adults dress as ordinary people and carry out mundane tasks, playful and a little offbeat. And Maja Baska has photographed Halloween in North Katoomba in the Blue Mountains with an analogue camera, moving between the everyday and the unsettling, with witches, clowns and a killer durian. It's documentary photography rather than fine art, but good for a quick, visual look.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope you find a quiet moment to look at something beautiful today.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It is Sunday the first of November, and this morning's art news has a pleasing mix of Grenoble lectures close to home, a few paintings seen through new eyes, and some stories where art and writing run into one another.

Let me start at home, at the Musée de Grenoble, where the next few days are busy with talks. The first is tomorrow, Monday the second of November, at half past two in the afternoon. It is a lecture for the Friends of the Museum, free to attend, titled "Le Caire: La Victorieuse ou La Martiale". The listing gives us the title and the time but not much more, so I can't tell you what the talk will argue. Even so, a lecture devoted to one work in the collection is a rare chance to slow down. If you have an hour tomorrow afternoon, it might be worth spending it in front of a single piece, with someone who has thought about it for a long time.

The second talk comes a couple of days later, on Wednesday the fourth of November, at half past six in the evening, again for the Friends of the Museum. It is called "L'Apocalypse de Saint Jean: Visions, Terreur… et Consolation". The Book of Revelation is read here through three words: visions, terror and consolation. I like that last one in particular, because we tend to remember the beasts and the trumpets and forget that the text is meant to comfort as well as frighten. For a literature teacher, it is a fine example of how a sacred text can pour itself into images, and how a piece of writing can be so vivid that painters have returned to it again and again. The evening hour also makes it a reasonable option after a day in the classroom, though I know the road down from Les Adrets in the dark is its own consideration at this time of year.

Looking a little further ahead, the museum has an event called "Clair-Obscur avec Ici-Même", with the collective Ici-Même, running from Monday the twenty-third to Sunday the twenty-ninth of November. The listing is sparse, with dates and a title and little else. But a title like Clair-Obscur, light and shadow, in a museum full of paintings, is one to keep in the diary. I'd suggest checking the museum's own programme nearer the time for details.

One small note on something you have just missed. Yesterday, Saturday the thirty-first of October, at half past four in the afternoon, the museum offered its short flash visits of the collection, open to everyone. That has gone by now, but it is a reminder that the museum runs quick, informal ways into the collection, and they may well be worth watching for on a free afternoon.

Closer to your own mountains, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports from Lans-en-Vercors, where the festival "Y'a tout ça" is continuing in the form of an exhibition. The report is brief, so I can't give you much on what is shown or for how long. But it is a Vercors event, not far from you, and the sort of small local show that often turns out to be the most charming kind. A look at the Dauphiné Libéré or the commune's own pages should fill in the practical details.

Now to the wider world of painting, starting with one of the most famous canvases ever made. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's "The Starry Night". It is a lovely idea: that behind those spinning, swirling heavens, which feel so entirely the product of one man's feeling, there may be an actual sky, one that could be matched with what astronomers can calculate. I should be honest that the report says "may have inspired", so this is a careful claim rather than a closed case. But whatever one makes of the science, it invites us to look again at a picture so familiar that we have almost stopped seeing it. For a classroom, I can imagine it working beautifully alongside poetry about stars and night, asking whether a painting is a record of what the artist saw, or of what he felt, or whether the two can ever be separated.

Staying with painting, there are two more items which are quite thin, but worth a mention. The first, from the site jds.fr, covers a digital-museum exhibition called "L'Impressionnisme: sur les traces de Claude Monet", following the Impressionist's path. The text we have is slight, so I can only say it exists and what its title promises. If you enjoy the idea of following a painter's footsteps, the title suggests exactly that. The second is a report that there is a major exhibition devoted to Tintoretto at the Musée Jacquemart-André in Paris. Again, the item is short, and I don't have dates or the contents of the show, so I would not plan a trip on this alone. But Tintoretto, the great Venetian master of drama and movement and strange, dazzling light, is always worth keeping an eye on, and it might sit nicely in a future Paris weekend once you've confirmed the dates.

Now for where art and literature meet, which I know is your favourite ground. The Guardian's week in art round-up carries the cheerful headline "Big hair with the pre-Raphaelites, seventeen Orkney stand-outs and night frights in Derry". Within it, the Fitzwilliam Museum in Cambridge is showing an exhibition on late Victorian art and politics, featuring William Morris and the pre-Raphaelites, and it runs until the third of May. I find it a particularly rich subject, because these were artists who couldn't keep painting, poetry, design and political conviction in separate rooms. Morris wrote and designed and argued; the pre-Raphaelites painted scenes from poems and legends, and often their models were as caught up in the stories as the pictures were. If you teach Victorian texts, an exhibition that shows them in the company of the images and objects of their moment is exactly the kind of thing that teaches history better than an essay. Since it runs through to May, there is time to plan a visit, or at least to browse the exhibition's material online for ideas to bring into class. The same round-up also nods to Orkney and to Derry, though the details we have are limited to those headline teasers.

On the literary side, the BBC Radio 4 programme Front Row has an episode which I think you'd enjoy. Audrey Niffenegger talks about "Life Out of Order", the sequel to her hugely successful novel "The Time Traveller's Wife". It returns to the time-travelling father and daughter, so we are once again in that strange territory where love and time pull in different directions. The novel gave us two memorable narrative voices and a structure that played with chronology in a way that students tend to find fascinating, and a sequel raises the always interesting question of what happens when an author goes back into a world that readers have already made their own. The same episode also includes Kyle MacLachlan's memoir, and a segment on Dracula's long literary history, which I'd say is a nice thing to listen to on a late autumn evening, with Halloween only just behind us. Dracula, after all, is a novel told entirely through letters, diaries and clippings, which makes it a gift for anyone who loves narrators.

From there, I'd like to turn to the longest and most thought-provoking read of the day. The Guardian has a substantial feature on Geoffrey Bardon and the painters of Papunya, under the title "A whitewashing of minds: the mania and myth of Geoffrey Bardon and the painting men of Papunya". It examines the myth surrounding the origins of Western Desert Aboriginal dot painting, an art movement whose beginnings have often been told through the figure of Bardon, the teacher who is said to have encouraged it. A new biography is the prompt for the reassessment. What I find compelling is that the piece is really about who gets to tell the story of an art movement, and how a founding legend can crowd out the people who actually made the work. It is a question that belongs as much to literature as to painting: whose voice carries the narrative, and whose is quietly written out. It could make for a very good discussion with older students about reliable and unreliable storytellers, even when the story is about art rather than fiction.

Finally, a handful of lighter pieces in photography, which makes for a gentle ending. The Guardian's series has Mark McEvoy describing his best phone picture. He took it in a Margate shop in 2014, of a young woman in a fur coat, and he says that a gust of wind blowing back her hair added something special. I like that very much: a whole photograph depending on a moment's chance, and a reminder that the best images are often partly given to us rather than made. It is a short and human story.

Two more photo essays from the Guardian carry a Halloween theme, and both are mainly pictures. One looks at Japan's "Jimi Halloween", a Tokyo event where, instead of dressing as witches and monsters, adults dress as ordinary people and perform mundane tasks. It is playful and gently odd, a celebration of all things mundane, which is a rather nice idea for a holiday so often about the extraordinary. The other is by Maja Baska, who documents Halloween in North Katoomba, in the Blue Mountains of Australia, using an analogue camera. She moves between the everyday and the unsettling, with witches, clowns and a killer durian among the cast. It is documentary photography rather than fine art, so think of it as a light, visual read, perhaps with a cup of tea.

That is the art news for this Sunday, Yamuna, and I hope something here sends you off to look at a painting a little more slowly.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a Shakespeare-and-Orwell sort of weekend in the BFI corner, with a little Atwood, a little Ishiguro and a Dickens house to finish on.

Let's begin with the stage, since Hamlet is on the 2027 programme. Two outlets have released images from Hamlet Hail to the Thief at the Barbican in London. West End Theatre has published first-look pictures of the new staging. Theatre Weekly has behind-the-scenes photography as previews begin. I can't tell you much about the production itself from these pieces, but the photographs could be useful in class. You might show your students a few frames and ask what the staging seems to emphasise, before they've heard a single line. It's a quick way into the question of how a director reads a play they think they already know.

Staying with Shakespeare, there is a cluster of pieces about performance and scholarship. Patrick Stewart is being marked as he takes what Everything Zoomer calls his final bow, in a feature tracing his career from Shakespeare to Star Trek. The Guardian has an appreciation of his stage work, headlined as bringing virile star power to the stage, from clowns to kings to wounded lions. I only have the headline, but that range, clowns and kings, sits nicely with both Twelfth Night and Hamlet. It might prompt a good discussion of how one actor can move between comedy and tragedy. In a more reflective vein, The Chronicle of Higher Education has an opinion essay asking, "Am I One of the Last Shakespeareans?" Again I only have the title, but a literature teacher may enjoy it for its own sake. For the dance lover in you, SeeingDance reports on Ballett Zürich's new A Midsummer Night's Dream, choreographed by Cathy Marston. Details are scarce, but it's one to look out for. And UPI has an "On This Day" item marking the debut of Othello in England, a handy hook if you want to open a lesson with a little theatre history.

Now to Orwell, who dominates the oral themes list this weekend. Three pieces touch on 1984. The Herald and News carries an op-ed arguing that the novel was a warning, not an instruction manual. That's a tidy provocation for discussing what Orwell was actually trying to do, and whether the book's purpose is to frighten, to caution, or to teach us how to notice. Searchlight Magazine has reviewed two stage pieces. One is Orwell: the Road to 1984 by Guy Smith, a play about the path leading to the novel. The review may offer some context for how Orwell arrived at the book, which would help students place it. The other is a review of Chris Hannan's stage adaptation of 1984. I should be honest that the text I have of that review is thin, so I can't say how the adaptation works. Still, the existence of a stage version gives you a comparison point: what changes when Winston's inner life is put in front of an audience?

Next, Margaret Atwood, whose The Handmaid's Tale is also on the oral list. Three items this weekend. The Peterborough Examiner has an opinion piece weighing which of Atwood's works still matter, prompted by her memoir covering five decades of writing. I only have the headline, but "which works still matter" is a good question to put to students: does The Handmaid's Tale earn its place, and why? ABC News has an item on The Testaments, exploring a new coming-of-age story in Gilead, with Chase Infiniti among the cast. Again only the headline, but a coming-of-age angle could help younger students see the Gilead stories through a character their own age. The Observer carries an opinion piece headlined, "Gilead is not fiction. It is coming for all women again today." I only have the headline, and it is politically charged, so I would use it with some care, perhaps as an example of how a novel gets pulled into present-day argument, rather than as a text to agree or disagree with.

Then a single but rewarding item on Kazuo Ishiguro. NPR has an interview in which he discusses Klara and the Sun and his approach to writing novels about the future. Klara and the Sun is not on your programme, but Never Let Me Go is on the oral list, and hearing the author talk about how he imagines the future could give your students a way to think about that novel's quiet, restrained version of science fiction. If NPR's interview is available as audio, it might make a short listening exercise.

Lastly, something for the Great Expectations shelf, which is on the 2027 programme. The Times of India reports on a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year. A three point two million pound restoration has removed later alterations. It's a pleasing link between a real London address and the author your seconde and première students may be reading. A photograph of the house could make a nice opening for a lesson on how Dickens's London was lived in, not just described.

That's the corner for today, and I hope the Hamlet photographs make a good start to the week.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet-ish weekend for the BFI corner, but there's a lot of Shakespeare, a good deal of Orwell and Atwood, and a couple of lovely things to carry into the classroom.

Let me begin with Hamlet, since it's on the twenty twenty-seven programme and there's news from London. Two outlets have published pictures from Hamlet Hail to the Thief, which is at the Barbican. West End Theatre has released first-look images of the new staging, and Theatre Weekly has followed with behind-the-scenes photography as previews begin. I should be honest that what we have here is the pictures and the announcements, rather than any detailed account of the directing choices. Still, that's enough to be useful. Production photographs are a wonderful way into a text with première students. You could put two or three images on the board without any caption and ask them to work out what the staging is saying: who is standing where, how the light falls, what the costumes suggest about the world of Elsinore. Then you read the corresponding scene together and ask whether the image honours the language or argues with it. For students who find Hamlet remote, seeing that it is still being reimagined, right now, in a major London theatre, can shift it from a set text to a living thing. And once the previews turn into full reviews, there may be more to say about how the production reads the play, so it's worth keeping an eye out.

Staying with Shakespeare for a moment, there is a cluster of pieces about performance and the people who devote their lives to it. The Guardian has published an appreciation of Patrick Stewart's stage work, under a headline that speaks of virile star power on the stage, from clowns to kings to wounded lions. I only have the headline, but it's a lovely phrase, and it describes quite a range: comic roles, royal roles, and those wounded older figures. Alongside it, Everything Zoomer has a feature on Stewart taking his final bow, tracing a path from Shakespeare to Star Trek. That one is described as a warm profile of a stage actor. Taken together, they could make a gentle, accessible lesson on how one actor can inhabit very different Shakespearean registers. With Twelfth Night and Hamlet both on the twenty twenty-seven list, there's a natural pairing: the clown and the king, the comic and the tragic. You might ask students what it means for an actor to play a fool and a prince in the same career, and whether the same skills are at work. It also gives you a way to talk about the idea that a character is not fixed on the page, but rediscovered by each performer.

Then there is a more reflective piece. The Chronicle of Higher Education has an opinion essay with the headline, Am I One of the Last Shakespeareans? Again, I only have the headline, so I can't tell you where the author lands. But the question itself is interesting for a teacher of literature, because it touches on whether deep, sustained attention to Shakespeare is under threat, and who carries it forward. It might be a good private read rather than a classroom text, though one could imagine posing the question to older students in a light way: is Shakespeare still essential, and why? Their answers might surprise you.

And for something that combines your love of dance with your love of Shakespeare, SeeingDance reports on Ballett Zürich's new A Midsummer Night's Dream, choreographed by Cathy Marston. The detail is thin, just the headline, so I can't describe the choreography or the casting. But a Shakespeare comedy turned into dance is a lovely thing to know about. It isn't on the programme, but it opens up a neat question for any class: what happens to a play when you take away the words? How do you show Puck, or the confusion of the lovers, or the transformation in the wood, using only bodies and music? You could use the same question for Twelfth Night, which is on the programme and has its own mistaken identities and music. Ask students how they'd stage Viola's disguise without a single line of dialogue. It's a good exercise in understanding how much the language is doing.

One more date-related Shakespeare item. UPI has an On This Day piece marking the date Othello debuted in England. Only the headline is available, so I won't add detail. But if you teach Shakespeare, a small anniversary hook like this can be a pleasant opening to a lesson, a way of reminding students that these plays were first performed in front of real audiences, on particular days, in particular places.

Now to the oral themes list, where Orwell has a strong showing. There are three items. First, Herald and News carries an op-ed arguing that Nineteen Eighty-Four was a warning, not an instruction manual. It's a crisp idea, and an effective prompt for discussion of the novel's purpose. You could ask students to take a side. What does it mean to say that a book is a warning? Who is being warned, and about what? And is a warning still a warning if people start to treat it as a blueprint? That question gets students thinking about authorial intention and about how readers use books, which is excellent oral preparation.

Second, Searchlight Magazine has reviewed a play called Orwell: the Road to 1984, by Guy Smith. It's about the path that led to Orwell's novel. Third, Searchlight has also reviewed a stage adaptation of Nineteen Eighty-Four by Chris Hannan. I should say that the text supplied for the second review is thin, so I can't tell you how either production fares. But the pairing is interesting. One play looks at how the book came to be, and the other adapts the book itself. For teaching, that gives you two different relationships to the same text: context before the novel, and interpretation after it. Students preparing for the oral could benefit from both. The first might help them think about the writer behind the book, and the pressures that shaped it. The second raises the question of what changes when a novel is staged: how do you dramatise a mind under surveillance, or the interior experience of Winston? If you're building a short sequence, you might start with the op-ed, move to a passage of the novel, and then ask what a theatre version would have to keep and what it would have to lose.

Atwood now, and three items for The Handmaid's Tale. The Observer has an opinion piece under the headline, Gilead is not fiction, it is coming for all women again today. The text I have is only the headline, and it is politically charged, so I'd treat it with care. It's an argument about the present, and your sixth-formers may have strong feelings either way. If you use it, I'd suggest it as an example of how a novel can be invoked in public debate, rather than as a statement to be agreed with. The literary question is a good one: why does Gilead keep being used as a reference point? What is it about Atwood's construction of that world that makes people reach for it? That keeps the focus on how the book works, which is where you'll want it for the oral.

Second, the Peterborough Examiner has an opinion piece prompted by Atwood's memoir, which covers five decades of her career. The headline invites us to weigh the works that still matter. Again, it's only a headline, but it offers a good angle. Which of an author's books survive, and why? You might ask students whether The Handmaid's Tale would be on that list, and what they would say to defend it.

Third, ABC News has an item on The Testaments, which explores a new coming-of-age story in Gilead, with Chase Infiniti among the cast. I only have the headline, so I can't say more about the adaptation. But the phrase coming-of-age is worth noting, because it suggests a younger point of view on that world. That could connect to a discussion of narrators: how does the story change when the person telling it is young and has grown up inside the system, rather than remembering a time before? That is a question about voice, and it's one you could put to the original novel as well, thinking about Offred's retrospective, fragmentary narration.

Next, Ishiguro. NPR has an interview with Kazuo Ishiguro about Klara and the Sun and his approach to writing novels about the future. Never Let Me Go is on the oral list, so this is a strong teaching link, and I think it's the most substantial item of the weekend for your purposes. Ishiguro talking about how he approaches the future in fiction may help students see that Never Let Me Go is not really about technology, but about people and how they cope with what they're given. That's a distinction that students often miss at first, expecting a science fiction novel and finding something quieter and sadder. Hearing the author talk about his method could unsettle that expectation in a productive way. If the interview is available as audio, it might make a lovely short listening exercise: play a few minutes, ask students to note what he says about the future, and then compare it with Kathy's narration. Her voice, calm, measured, almost evasive, is one of the most memorable in contemporary fiction, and it's very much in your territory of strong narrators.

Finally, something for the seconde and première classes who may be meeting Dickens, and good for anyone who loves the way literature and place go together. The Times of India has a piece about a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year, and a three point two million pound restoration that removed later alterations. I don't have more detail than that, but the idea is wonderful: a physical building stripped back, as far as possible, to what Dickens would have known. Great Expectations is on the twenty twenty-seven programme, and it's a novel so concerned with houses, with Miss Havisham's decaying rooms, the forge, Wemmick's little castle, that a story about restoring a real Dickens residence is a charming bridge. You could ask students why we want to preserve the places where writers lived, and whether seeing a room changes how we read the books. And then, more specifically, you might ask them to look at how Dickens describes interiors, and what a house tells us about the person living in it. It's the sort of connection between place and text that tends to stay with students.

So, to gather it up. For Hamlet, the Barbican images are your visual prompt. For Orwell, you have a ready-made question about warnings, and two stage pieces to think about adaptation. For Atwood, there's plenty to discuss, though with a careful hand on the political material. For Ishiguro, the NPR interview is the one I'd listen to first. And for Dickens, there's a small, pleasing story about a house.

Enjoy the rest of your Sunday, and may all your Elsinores be well lit.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's Sunday the first of November, and this morning's round-up is mostly a look ahead: the Grenoble stages are filling up for the weeks to come, with a few nearer to home to keep in mind.

Let's begin with today, since there is something on right now. This Sunday, the first of November, there is a guided visit at the Maison Bergès, the Musée de la Houille blanche, in Villard-Bonnot. It's called "La force de l'eau, la force de l'art", the strength of water, the strength of art, and it links the history of hydroelectric power with art. The listing describes it as a regular guided visit, so if today doesn't work, it may well come round again. It sits neatly with your taste for places where industry and imagination meet, and it's right down in the Grésivaudan, not far from you. I haven't been given a time, so a quick check before setting off would be wise.

Also in the category of things that last: in Allevard there is a free temporary exhibition called "L'avant de l'après", which can be visited until the thirty-first of October next year. The listing gives no more detail than that, so I can't tell you what it contains. But a free show with a whole year to run is the sort of thing you can keep in your back pocket for a quiet weekend, perhaps combined with a stroll around Allevard itself. No rush at all.

Now to the part of the news that is busiest, which is Wednesday the fourth of November, when three different things are happening in two places.

First, at MC2 in Grenoble, there is a ciné-concert called "Le Sommet des dieux", the summit of the gods. It features Patrick Imbert, with the Orchestre national Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes conducted by Jean Deroyer. The idea of a ciné-concert is that a film is shown while an orchestra plays the music live, so the score is not a recording but something happening in the room, breathing with the images. Given your love of classical music and of documentaries about it, this one seems a natural fit. I'm afraid the listing doesn't say more about the film or the programme, so it's worth a look at the MC2 page for the details.

Second, on the same day, the fourth, and continuing on the fifth, MC2 hosts Betty Tchomanga with her dance piece "The Sea is History". The title is, of course, borrowed in spirit from the idea of the sea as a keeper of memory, though I should be honest that the listing itself is brief and doesn't describe the piece. What I can tell you is that it's contemporary dance, and that it runs for two evenings, so you have a little flexibility.

Third, and in a different spot altogether, Allevard is offering a new writing and creative workshop led by Véronique Buthod, also on the fourth of November. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports it, though the text gives no further details, so I can't say the hours, the cost or whether it's aimed at beginners. As someone who spends her days with other people's sentences, you may find it appealing to be on the making end for an afternoon. It might also be a pleasant thing to mention to a colleague or a keen student, if you know of someone who writes. Do check with the organisers before planning around it.

The following day, Thursday the fifth of November, MC2 in Grenoble has what it calls a préambule, a preliminary talk, with Marion Grange, on the memory of the transatlantic slave trade. A préambule is a kind of introduction, given ahead of a larger event, and here the subject is serious and historically rich. This is the sort of thing that speaks to your interest in how culture carries history, and in how novels and stories can teach what essays sometimes can't. The listing doesn't say which performance or programme it leads into, but it is presumably connected to the MC2 season. It could be a useful evening for thinking about texts you teach in the British section, though that is only a thought of mine, not something the listing claims.

Moving on to music, there is a good run of concerts through November, and I'll take them in date order.

On Sunday the eighth of November, at MC2 in Grenoble, the pianist David Kadouch gives a concert titled "Amours interdites", forbidden loves. A Sunday classical concert with a title like that suggests a programme with a story running through it, though the listing itself doesn't spell out what he will play, so I won't guess. It's the first of several MC2 evenings that I think you would enjoy, and a Sunday is always a gentler time to go into town.

On Friday the thirteenth of November, again at MC2, there is "L'Antidote", a world music concert with three musicians together on stage: Bijan Chemirani, Redi Hasa and Rami Khalifé. It's a strong line-up, and the pairing of names promises a meeting of traditions rather than a single sound. The listing gives only the names and the genre, so that is all I can say, but it looks like a rich evening.

On Thursday the nineteenth of November, MC2 hosts "Último helecho", which is Spanish for something like "last fern". It is a music performance by Nina Laisné, François Chaignaud and Nadia Larcher. The listing offers no description at all beyond the names and the title, so it's one for the curious. If you like to be surprised, perhaps that's no bad thing.

And on Thursday the twenty-sixth of November, the jazz musician Anne Paceo plays "Atlantis" at MC2. It's a live concert, and a little further off, so there's time to plan. If you fancy something other than classical, it's a pleasant change of colour in the month's programme.

The text I have doesn't give the date, so I can't tell you when it is. Given your ear for musical prose and for the older repertoire, it looks worth tracking down, but please check the listing before you book anything, because the date is the one thing missing.

Now for theatre, which is where your two worlds, the classroom and the evening out, come closest together.

On the twelfth and thirteenth of November, at MC2 in Grenoble, there is Beaumarchais' play "La Folle Journée ou le mariage de Figaro", in a staging by Lucile Lacaze. It's a classic text, and one that you could very naturally bring into your literature classes, whether as a point of comparison with the English comic tradition or simply as a lively example of a play that has a great deal to say about its time. The listing doesn't say more about Lucile Lacaze's approach, so I can't tell you whether it is traditional or bold, but seeing a production of a text you know is always interesting for a teacher, and a good talking point afterwards. Note that the thirteenth is also the evening of "L'Antidote", so you would have to choose between them, or take the twelfth for Figaro.

Then on the nineteenth and twentieth of November, MC2 presents "L'Ange du foyer", the angel of the hearth, a theatre production by Emma Dante. Her work is worth knowing, as the listing itself notes, though it gives no more detail about this particular piece. The nineteenth, again, overlaps with "Último helecho", so you will have a choice to make that evening, and the twentieth is the alternative.

On the subject of visual art, there is one item for you, on Saturday the fourteenth of November, at the Musée de Grenoble. It is a visite tactile, a touch tour, organised through the MC2's accessibility programme. The idea is that visitors can experience the museum through touch, in an inclusive format. The listing doesn't say which works are involved or who the tour is designed for beyond that, but it is a different and rather thoughtful way of meeting art in a place you may already know well. If you have ever wanted to see a familiar museum from a new angle, this may be it. Do check the booking arrangements, as tours of this kind are often small.

Finally, a piece of good news, which I know you like. Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that a man from the Sud-Grésivaudan area is going back to Indonesia to protect elephants. The text I have is short, so I can't tell you his name or what exactly he will be doing, but the headline alone is a hopeful local story about conservation, with someone from our own valley carrying a commitment across the world. If you'd like the full story, it's worth looking for the article.

Let me pull the dates together so you can plan. Today, Sunday the first, there is the Maison Bergès visit in Villard-Bonnot. On Wednesday the fourth, you have the ciné-concert and the first night of "The Sea is History" at MC2, plus the writing workshop in Allevard. On Thursday the fifth, the talk with Marion Grange and the second night of the dance. Sunday the eighth brings David Kadouch. The twelfth and thirteenth are Figaro, and the thirteenth also has "L'Antidote". The fourteenth is the touch tour at the Musée de Grenoble. The nineteenth and twentieth bring "L'Ange du foyer", with "Último helecho" on the nineteenth, and the twenty-sixth is Anne Paceo. The polyphony concert and the Allevard exhibition remain open-ended, so keep those two for when you have a free moment.

A final note: much of this comes from short listings, so for times, prices and booking, the MC2 pages and the organisers' own sites will be the place to confirm.

So, a month of good evenings is taking shape down in the valley, and I hope you find one that suits you, Yamuna.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's the first of November, and the last two days have brought a gentle crop of good news, with plenty of paintings, words and small kindnesses in it.

Let me start with a few things that might send you back to a canvas or a page. Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. It's a lovely link between painting and astronomy, and an invitation to look again at those swirling skies, perhaps with a class, asking how much of the sky is observed and how much imagined. Then, from The Times of India, there's a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year. A restoration costing three point two million pounds has now removed the later alterations. If your seconde or première students are reading Dickens, a house you can picture him walking out of may bring him a little closer.

On the subject of writing, ARTE has a documentary I think you'd enjoy, called À la recherche de l'écriture oubliée. The archaeologist François Desset describes how, after fifteen years of research, he deciphered Elamite linear script, a writing system from southern Iran that is more than four thousand years old and was long thought unreadable. It's a proper piece of linguistic detective work, and it's available to watch until April next year. Staying with schools, also from Good News Network, two Florida teachers, Maren and David Douglass, noticed that a schoolgirl's bus stop was at the end of their driveway, and that she was sitting in the dirt while she waited. Sébastien Roca is a cemetery keeper, and he talks about how families confide in him and tell him their stories when they come to honour their dead. He says he feels useful to others. Barbara had moved to Oscott Retirement Village in Birmingham, and it seems that was the start of something new. And from Upworthy, an eighty-five-year-old woman in a senior home sang a cover of Fleetwood Mac's Landslide and, as they put it, brought down the house. The whole room was moved. He Ziqi, now a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence, was admitted to a prestigious university partly because of a strawberry farmer, whose phone number happened to appear on a middle-school English exam question. And The Optimist Daily's podcast of the thirtieth of October features Vivian Ho, a teenager who built a supply network where families can request goods without filling in any forms. She also sends handmade crafts that reflect each family's cultural background, so the help comes with a small gesture of recognition. The same episode touches on a wildlife deal in Kenya, and on electric vehicles and energy security.

Both have now been removed, the island is flourishing again, and the coral reefs offshore have recovered too. The article is brief, but it's a clear case of a repair that worked. Nearer home, Le Dauphiné Libéré says a man from the Sud-Grésivaudan is returning to Indonesia to protect elephants. The text I have is short, but it's pleasing to think of a neighbour from the valley doing that work.

So, from a starry sky to a stubborn island, I hope there's something here to carry into your Sunday, perhaps with a walk and a good book.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's the first of November, a quiet, reflective sort of Sunday, and the good news this morning is full of stars, old scripts, kind strangers and one very moving song.

Let me begin with paintings, writing and words, since they seem to be gathering today.

Beaux Arts Magazine reports that scientists have identified the night sky that may have inspired Van Gogh's The Starry Night. The wording is careful, and rightly so: it is the sky that may have inspired the painting. But what I like is the invitation it offers. A canvas you may have shown a class many times, with its churning blue and those swollen, haloed stars, is suddenly tied to something one could in principle look up and find. It sets two kinds of looking side by side, the astronomer's and the painter's. If you ever teach a lesson on how writers and artists transform what they see, it's a lovely hook. Is the swirling sky observation, or is it feeling? Perhaps the honest answer is both.

From a painted sky to a very old piece of writing. On ARTE, the archaeologist François Desset describes how, after fifteen years of research, he deciphered Elamite linear script. This is a writing system from southern Iran, more than four thousand years old, which was long thought unreadable. The film is called In Search of the Forgotten Writing, and it is a proper piece of detective work, the sort where patience is the main tool. Fifteen years is a long time to stay with a puzzle that many people believed had no solution. There is something rather moving in the thought that a voice, or at least a set of marks that once meant something to someone, can be brought back after four millennia. It's available to watch until April next year, so there is no rush, and it might make a good evening's viewing once the clocks have settled.

Closer to your own classroom, the Times of India has a piece about a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year. It has just had a restoration costing three point two million pounds, which removed later alterations. I like the idea of stripping away the layers that came afterwards, to get closer to the house as the writer knew it. For students in seconde and première who may be meeting Dickens, or will soon, a real address in London makes the novels feel less like furniture in a museum. Someone rented a house, paid his rent, and wrote there. That is the sort of detail that brings a Victorian author down to earth.

There is also a literary prize to mention. The South African novelist Damon Galgut has won the Park Kyung-ni Prize, a Korean literary award, according to the Korea Herald. The report I have is little more than a headline, so I can't tell you more about the ceremony. But it is pleasing to see a Booker-winning writer honoured again, and by a prize from a different literary world. It's a small reminder of how books travel.

And on the subject of language, Upworthy has a piece on a linguist who shows how English expressions such as "by the way" and "of course" reveal an underlying metaphor: that thinking is walking. Think about it. A "way", a "course": we speak of ideas as if they were paths we take. The piece itself is brief, but the idea is the sort of thing that could occupy ten delightful minutes with a class. Ask them to hunt for other phrases where thought is a journey, where we go off on a tangent, lose the thread, or arrive at a conclusion. Once you notice it, you can't stop noticing it.

Finally in this corner, a note from the history column at Good News Network. Yesterday, the thirty-first of October, was the anniversary of the birth of the British-Iraqi architect Zaha Hadid, seventy-six years ago. The piece recalls her knighthood and her London firm, which continues to innovate. For someone who loves the way paintings and buildings and books talk to one another, she is a fitting figure to remember, an architect whose work seemed to flow rather than stand still.

Now to the natural world, where there are two stories of things coming back.

Upworthy tells of a Caribbean island that had come to look like a moonscape, barren and stripped, after goats and rats were introduced. Both have now been removed, and the island is flourishing again. The coral reefs offshore have recovered too. The text is short, so I can't give you the island's name or the numbers, but the shape of the story is clear and encouraging. Damage that people did, other people have undone. And the way the reefs recovered as well is a good reminder that what happens on land can reach all the way into the sea.

On a much more local note, Le Dauphiné Libéré reports that a man from the Sud-Grésivaudan is going back to Indonesia to protect elephants. The article I have is short, so I don't know the details of his work, but it is nice to think that someone from your own corner of the Isère is carrying that commitment so far from home. If you do get the chance to read the full piece over a coffee, I suspect it will be worth it.

Next, a handful of stories about small kindnesses, and about people who are too rarely thanked.

Today being Toussaint, franceinfo has a portrait of Sébastien Roca, a cemetery keeper in Grenoble. He talks about how families come to honour their dead and how they confide in him and tell him their stories. He says he feels useful to others. It's a gentle piece, and it fits this particular day so well. We tend to think of a cemetery keeper as someone who looks after stones and paths, but he describes the work as looking after people, listening to them at one of the most tender moments there is. There is a quiet dignity in that, and it is lovely that his work is being noticed on the very day when so many families visit.

Another kind of recognition comes from Texas, where Good News Network reports that a school district has named a new school after Marilyn Hampton, a longtime custodian known to everyone as Miss Marilyn. The honour moved her deeply, and there is a video of her reaction for anyone who wants a lift. I find this one especially touching, because the work of a school caretaker is so often invisible. Schools run on people like her, who arrive before the children and leave after them. To have a building carry your name for generations is about as lasting a thank-you as one could imagine.

And then Florida. Good News Network tells the story of two teachers, Maren and David Douglass, whose driveway ends at a school bus stop. They noticed a schoolgirl sitting in the dirt while she waited, and surprised her with a bench. The kindness went viral, and the video shows her delight, with, apparently, a little jig of happiness. It was a very simple gift, and it solved a very small problem that someone had actually noticed. I like that the people who did it are teachers. You'll know that the instinct to see a child waiting and think "that can't be comfortable" is a teacher's instinct through and through.

Now, two stories about people in later life, which I think you will enjoy.

Good News Network reports that Barbara Thompson and Fred Jenkins, both widowed, have fallen in love again at eighty-eight. They met at the gym, after Barbara moved to Oscott Retirement Village in Birmingham. I'm not going to embroider it, because it doesn't need it. Two people who had each lost a spouse, each in their late eighties, found one another among the exercise machines. It is a reminder that life keeps its surprises well past the age when people assume the plot is settled. Any novelist would be glad of a pair of characters like that.

And from Upworthy, an eighty-five-year-old woman in a senior home sang a cover of Fleetwood Mac's Landslide and, in the words of the headline, brought down the house. The whole room was moved. It is a song about time, change and growing older, and I can only imagine how it sounded in the voice of someone eighty-five. I don't have more detail about who she is, but the story is about that shared silence in a room when a song lands properly. If you ever find yourself at a village concert or a small gathering up in the Belledonne, you'll recognise that feeling.

To close the main run of stories, two about the young, and about how far a small act can travel.

Good News Network has a delightful tale about He Ziqi, who is now a postgraduate student in artificial intelligence. He was admitted to a prestigious university, partly, as reported, thanks to a strawberry farmer whose phone number happened to appear on a middle-school English exam. The farmer didn't know his number was in the exam question at all. Now he treats the calls he receives as opportunities to inspire others. I love how accidental it all is. A number printed on a test paper becomes a line between a farmer and a stream of students, and rather than being annoyed, he has made it a ministry of encouragement. An English exam doing this is of course close to your heart.

Lastly, The Optimist Daily's podcast from the thirtieth of October features Vivian Ho, a teenager who built a supply network where families can request goods without filling in forms. She also sends handmade crafts that reflect each family's cultural background. I find the second detail the most thoughtful: she isn't just sending things, she is sending something that says "we see where you come from." The same episode also touches on a wildlife deal in Kenya and on energy security for electric vehicles, though I only have the headlines of those.

So that's the morning: a sky that may have inspired a painting, a script read again after four thousand years, a bench, a school named for a caretaker, and an old voice that stopped a room, and I hope something here makes your Sunday a little lighter, Yamuna.

One for the list, and perhaps for a classroom conversation, since you'd be able to ask your students which standards of beauty they think are truly old and which are brand new.

And Radio Times has published its guide to what is coming to Netflix UK in November. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you what's in it, but it is worth a scan of the full list when you have a quiet moment, particularly for strong thrillers, literary adaptations or dance documentaries, which are exactly the things you would want to catch early.

So, if I had to pick a short list for the week: the Elamite script film on ARTE first, the DGSE series for the intrigue, the beauty documentary for its ideas, and the Déclics episode before the end of the month. Then, a little Mirlitons for sweetness, and the Strauss recording for the mountains.

Enjoy the quiet of the first of November, Yamuna, and may your evening be full of good stories.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Sunday, the first of November, which is Toussaint.

Let me start with books. Prospect Magazine has a piece on the many revolutions of John Berger, the writer who moved between art criticism, fiction and politics. The text I have is brief, but for someone who likes to hold a painting and a page side by side, it looks promising. Staying with writers and their ancestors, The Hindu has an interview with the novelist Elif Shafak about the kindred spirit she found in Gustave Flaubert, a conversation about how one novelist's life can quietly shape another's work.

In fiction, Gayety reviews Marlon James's Booker-shortlisted novel The Disappearers. It follows gay men in Kingston after an attack in nineteen eighty-eight, so it's a historical novel with a strong premise and a clear narrative focus, the sort that teaches history through character. Two more reviews from the New York Times. One is of Sound Tracks by Graeme Lawson, which tells a story of human music-making through ancient instruments, mixing music, archaeology and history. The other covers two new poetry collections leaning into the ecstatic, aiming for almost mystical effects, which sounds right for anyone who loves language as music.

On to art, and two Friends of the Museum lectures at the Musée de Grenoble, both free to attend. Tomorrow, Monday the second of November, at half past two in the afternoon, there is a talk on the Le Caire work called La Victorieuse, or La Martiale. It could be nice to look closely at the piece before you go. Then on Wednesday the fourth, at half past six in the evening, a lecture on the Book of Revelation, read as visions, terror and consolation. For a literature teacher, it's a good chance to think about how a sacred text has inspired images.

Closer to home, today at the Maison Bergès, the museum of hydroelectric power in Villard-Bonnot, there is a guided visit called La force de l'eau, la force de l'art. It links the history of hydroelectricity with art, which is a fitting pairing in the Grésivaudan. And on Wednesday the fourth, Le Dauphiné Libéré tells us of a new writing and creative workshop in Allevard, led by Véronique Buthod. The details are scarce, but given your love of writing, it may be worth a phone call.

In France, franceinfo has a gentle portrait from Grenoble for Toussaint. Sébastien Roca, a cemetery keeper, describes how families come to honour their dead and confide in him, telling him their stories. He says he feels useful to others, and it's a humane piece. Looking ahead, The Local France previews the week: children go back to school after the Toussaint holidays, there is a nationwide strike, a new motorway is due to open, and the winner of a major literature prize will be announced.

Something to watch and listen to now. The Guardian reviews Vasily Petrenko and the Royal Philharmonic's recording of Strauss's Alpine Symphony on Harmonia Mundi. The reviewer finds it expansive and vivid, and compares it with two other recent recordings, so it might be a pleasant pretext for a mountain-facing listen from your window. And on ARTE, there is a real piece of detective work. The archaeologist François Desset explains how, after fifteen years of research, he deciphered Elamite linear script, a writing system from southern Iran more than four thousand years old, long thought unreadable. It's available until April twenty twenty-seven, so there is no rush.

For your corner with the older students, The Times of India writes about a London house that Charles Dickens once rented for eighty pounds a year. A three point two million pound restoration has removed later alterations, which could be a vivid way to tie the author to a real place for your seconde and première classes. And Searchlight Magazine has a theatre review of Chris Hannan's stage adaptation of Orwell's 1984. The text I have is thin, but since the novel is on the oral list, a stage version may prove useful for teaching.

Now to finish with good news. The Good News Network tells of Barbara Thompson and Fred Jenkins, both widowed, who have fallen in love again at eighty-eight after meeting at the gym. Barbara had moved to Oscott Retirement Village in Birmingham. And Upworthy has an eighty-five-year-old woman in a senior home who brought down the house with a cover of Fleetwood Mac's Landslide, moving the whole room.

That's all for this morning, Yamuna. I hope your Sunday is full of good light over Belledonne, and a book within reach.
